claims.text: Annealing as-received Q235 steel at 800 °C produces a continuous and adherent near-surface oxide scale.
An optimum annealing duration produces an oxide scale that protects Q235 steel in both high-temperature molten salt and room-temperature aqueous environments.
Annealing durations outside the optimum produce either insufficient oxide coverage or overgrown, unstable scales.
Q235 steel is to be annealed at 800 °C for 1, 5, and 10 hours.
Annealing promotes elemental diffusion that assists formation of protective oxide phases in Q235 steel.
The post-annealing hot-corrosion test uses 75% Na2SO4 and 25% NaCl molten salt at 750 °C.
The post-annealing room-temperature test uses electrochemical measurements in NaCl solution.
The protective Q235 scale is predominantly composed of Fe oxides with minor spinel-type phases.
Scale continuity, density, uniformity, adhesion, thickness, and phase composition govern its barrier performance.
An optimal oxide layer reduces oxygen and ion ingress by acting as a physical barrier.
The oxide barrier reduces Q235 mass loss during molten-salt exposure.
The same annealing-induced oxide barrier maintains or enhances room-temperature passivation of Q235 steel.
Too little annealing leaves incomplete oxide coverage, whereas excessive annealing causes oxide overgrowth or spallation.
An intermediate annealing duration, likely about 5 hours, produces the most uniform and adherent scale.
The intermediate-duration sample will have significantly lower molten-salt mass loss than untreated Q235 steel.
The intermediate-duration sample will have comparable or slightly enhanced room-temperature passivation relative to untreated Q235 steel.
Short and excessively long annealing treatments will provide less corrosion resistance than the intermediate treatment.
Untreated, as-received Q235 steel is the control for both corrosion regimes.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to unalloyed and otherwise unmodified Q235 under the specified annealing and exposure conditions.
Absence of a relationship between annealing-dependent scale properties and improved corrosion performance would falsify the proposed scale-controlled mechanism.
